findings.description: File lock operation follows symbolic links without validation in SoftFileLock._acquire()
findings.reasoning: The os.open() call at line 27 in SoftFileLock._acquire() uses the O_EXCL flag which prevents following symlinks when creating new files. However, if a symlink already exists at self.lock_file path, os.open() will follow it and operate on the target file instead of the symlink itself. An attacker could create a symlink pointing to an arbitrary file (e.g., /etc/passwd or other critical files) and cause the lock operation to affect that file instead. The O_EXCL flag only prevents creation of new files but doesn't prevent following existing symlinks.

evidence.code_context: The SoftFileLock class uses os.open(self.lock_file, flags, self._context.mode) where flags include O_EXCL. While O_EXCL prevents creating files that already exist, it does not prevent following symlinks. If self.lock_file is a symlink, os.open() will follow it to the target file.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: self.lock_file is passed from the constructor without any symlink validation. The lock_file parameter comes directly from user input via BaseFileLock.__init__() and is stored in self._context.lock_file without any path normalization or symlink checks.
evidence.notes: The vulnerability exists because: 1) No check for symlinks before opening, 2) os.open() follows symlinks by default, 3) An attacker in a shared directory could create a symlink to arbitrary files, 4) The lock operation would then affect the target file instead of the intended lock file.

findings.description: File lock operation follows symbolic links without validation in UnixFileLock._acquire()
findings.reasoning: The UnixFileLock._acquire() method at line 44 uses os.open() to open the lock file. Although the code checks Path(self.lock_file).exists() before opening, this check itself follows symlinks and creates a TOCTOU (Time-of-Check-Time-of-Use) race condition. An attacker could: 1) Create a symlink at the lock file path, 2) The exists() check passes (following the symlink), 3) Between the check and os.open(), replace the symlink with one pointing to a different file, 4) os.open() then follows the new symlink to an arbitrary file. Additionally, even without the race condition, if a symlink already exists, os.open() will follow it.

evidence.code_context: UnixFileLock._acquire() at line 44 calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode). The open_flags include O_CREAT which creates the file if it doesn't exist, but os.open() will follow symlinks when opening existing files.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: The lock_file path comes from self.lock_file which is derived from self._context.lock_file, set during initialization without any symlink validation. The Path(self.lock_file).exists() check at line 43 follows symlinks, creating a TOCTOU vulnerability.
evidence.notes: The vulnerability is compounded by: 1) Path.exists() follows symlinks, 2) os.open() follows symlinks, 3) No use of os.open() with O_NOFOLLOW flag, 4) Race condition between exists() check and open() call, 5) No symlink validation before any file operations.

findings.code_snippet:
def _release(self) -> None:
            # Do not remove the lockfile:
            #   https://github.com/tox-dev/py-filelock/issues/31
            #   https://stackoverflow.com/questions/17708885/flock-removing-locked-file-without-race-condition

This violates CWE-667 (Improper Locking) and CWE-662 (Improper Synchronization) as the lock is not properly released and the resource is not properly cleaned up.

This leaves the file descriptor open.

def _acquire(self) -> None:
        ensure_directory_exists(self.lock_file)

        with suppress(PermissionError):  # This locked is not owned by this UID
            os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode)
